market_context: United States; 2% cow's milk and fortified unsweetened soy beverage as reference products
title: Cow's milk vs. soy milk: protein, calcium and fat

seo.title: Cow's milk vs. soy milk: protein, calcium and fat
seo.meta_description: Fortified soy milk comes closest to dairy milk nutritionally. A typical cup provides about 7 g protein and 300 mg calcium versus roughly 8 g and 290 mg in 2% milk; fortification and added sugar matter.
seo.search_intent: Compare dairy milk and fortified soy beverage for protein, calcium, fat and sugars while explaining product-to-product variation.

excerpt: Fortified unsweetened soy milk can come very close to cow's milk in protein and calcium. A cup of 2% dairy milk provides roughly 8 g protein and 290 mg calcium; the FDA's fortified plant-beverage example provides 7 g and 300 mg. Soy is typically lower in saturated fat and contains no lactose, but calcium and vitamin levels depend on fortification.
content_html:
Comparing dairy milk with “plant milk” as one category hides enormous differences among soy, oat, almond and rice beverages. Fortified soy is the plant option that most closely matches dairy milk for protein and several key nutrients, which makes it the useful comparison here.

Protein is surprisingly close

A USDA reference for 2% milk provides about 3.3 g protein per 100 g, or roughly 8 g in a cup. The FDA's example Nutrition Facts panel for a fortified plant beverage provides 7 g protein per 240 mL cup.

That is far closer than many other plant beverages, which can contain only a small fraction of dairy milk's protein. Still, soy brands differ, so check the label rather than assuming every carton supplies 7–8 g.

Calcium depends on fortification

Dairy milk naturally contains calcium: the 2% reference has around 120 mg per 100 g, about 290 mg per cup. The FDA's fortified beverage example lists 300 mg per cup.

The important difference is origin. Much of soy beverage's calcium is added during manufacturing, and unfortified products can contain substantially less. Minerals can also settle, so shake the carton when the label recommends it.

Total fat can be similar while saturated fat differs

The 2% dairy reference contains about 2 g total fat per 100 g. The FDA soy-style example contains 4 g per cup, about 1.7 g/100 mL, but only 0.5 g saturated fat in the whole cup.

Soy fat is predominantly unsaturated and contains no cholesterol. Dairy fat changes dramatically with the product: whole, 2%, 1% and skim milk should not be treated as nutritionally identical.

Lactose and added sugar are different questions

Dairy milk naturally contains lactose, contributing roughly 12 g total sugar per cup. Unsweetened soy can contain very little sugar, while flavored soy beverages may contain significant added sugar.

That makes the Added Sugars line especially useful when comparing U.S. labels.

Why fortified soy is different from most plant beverages

The FDA notes that fortified soy beverages are the plant-based alternative currently included with dairy in federal dietary guidance because their key nutrient profile is similar enough to milk. Almond, oat and rice beverages are not automatically nutritionally equivalent.

Neither choice wins every criterion. Dairy milk offers naturally occurring protein and micronutrients; fortified soy offers comparable protein and calcium with less saturated fat and no lactose. The specific carton still matters.

faq.question: Which has more protein, milk or soy milk?
faq.answer: They are close when soy is a conventional high-protein formula: roughly 8 g per cup for 2% dairy milk versus 7 g in the FDA fortified beverage example.

faq.question: Does soy milk have as much calcium as dairy milk?
faq.answer: Fortified products can. The FDA example has 300 mg per cup, but unfortified soy can contain much less.

faq.question: Is soy milk lactose-free?
faq.answer: Yes. Lactose is the natural sugar in mammalian milk and is not present in soy beverage.
